mechanicalFacts: The torso starts more pitched forward than a shorter-femur build — long thighs put the hips further back at setup.
Off the floor the hips tend to rise first while the torso stays pitched; this is the sticking point, not a fault to coach away.
The bar hangs under the shoulders the whole pull — that's the vertical path the arms track.
Lockout brings the torso to vertical as the hips finish through.
stanceCue: Lifters with this structure often set the hips a little higher — chasing a low, squat-style hip position fights the long-femur leverage.
irrelevantCue: "Get your hips down like a squat" → With long femurs, forcing the hips low shifts the shoulders behind the bar and lengthens the lever. The higher hip is the structure, not a shortcut.

mechanicalFacts: The torso sits closer to upright at setup — a shorter thigh and longer torso let the hips start lower without the bar drifting forward.
The knees bend more than a long-femur build, so the pull looks a little more squat-like off the floor.
The bar still hangs straight under the shoulders throughout the pull.
The sticking point off the floor is milder — the shoulders sit more over the bar from the start.
stanceCue: Lifters with this structure can usually start with the hips lower and the chest taller without losing the bar over mid-foot.
irrelevantCue: "Keep your hips high to save your back" → With short femurs, an exaggerated high hip turns the pull into a stiff-legged hinge the structure doesn't need.

mechanicalFacts: Setup torso lean sits between the long- and short-femur extremes for a balanced hip height.
Hips and shoulders rise at a similar rate off the floor, so the sticking point is moderate.
The bar tracks straight down from the shoulders through the whole pull.
The torso reaches vertical as the hips finish at lockout.
stanceCue: A hip-width stance with the bar over mid-foot and the shoulders just in front of the bar is a common starting point for this balanced proportion.
irrelevantCue: "There's one correct hip height for the deadlift" → Where the hips start depends on femur, torso, and arm length — a balanced build still has its own natural setup.

mechanicalFacts: A wider hip changes how the thighs clear the arms — the stance and grip often sit a touch wider to give the hips room.
Hip height and torso lean are otherwise close to a proportional build off the floor.
The bar still hangs straight under the shoulders through the pull.
Knee-out at setup is naturally greater to keep the shins clear of a wider hip.
stanceCue: Lifters with this structure often set a slightly wider stance so the hips can drop in without the thighs crowding the arms.
irrelevantCue: "Pull with a narrow, hip-width stance" → With a wider hip, a narrow stance crowds the arms against the thighs — a little more width is the natural fit, not a fault.
